title: Employment standards
intro: This guide describes, in general terms, what Ontario's Employment Standards Act, 2000 says about who it covers, some of the standards it sets, and how a complaint or a court case about those standards is started. It explains what the Act says; it does not say whether any standard applies to a particular job.

sections.heading: Who the Act covers
paragraphs: Subject to the exceptions in subsections (2) to (5), the employment standards in the Act apply to an employee and employer if “the employee's work is to be performed in Ontario”, or if the work is performed in Ontario and outside Ontario but “the work performed outside Ontario is a continuation of work performed in Ontario”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (1))

The Act “does not apply with respect to an employee and his or her employer if their employment relationship is within the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada.” It also lists other people it does not apply to, such as “A secondary school student who performs work under a work experience program authorized by the school board”, “A holder of political, religious or judicial office” and “Any prescribed individuals.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (2), (5))

The Act also says “An employer shall not treat, for the purposes of this Act, a person who is an employee of the employer as if the person were not an employee under this Act.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5.1 (1))

sections.heading: Standards cannot be signed away
paragraphs: Section 5 is headed “No contracting out”. It says “no employer or agent of an employer and no employee or agent of an employee shall contract out of or waive an employment standard and any such contracting out or waiver is void.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (1))

There is one exception. If one or more provisions in an employment contract or in another Act “that directly relate to the same subject matter as an employment standard provide a greater benefit to an employee than the employment standard”, then “the provision or provisions in the contract or Act apply and the employment standard does not apply.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (2))

sections.heading: Getting paid
paragraphs: “An employer shall establish a recurring pay period and a recurring pay day and shall pay all wages earned during each pay period, other than accruing vacation pay, no later than the pay day for that period.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (1))

When employment ends, the employer must pay any wages owing no later than the later of “seven days after the employment ends” and “the day that would have been the employee's next pay day.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (5))

The Act says “An employer shall pay employees at least the minimum wage.” Minimum wages are adjusted each October 1 by a formula using the Consumer Price Index, with no adjustment if it would result in a decrease. “The Minister shall, not later than April 1 of every year after 2021, publish on a website of the Government of Ontario the minimum wages that are to apply starting on October 1 of that year.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 23 (1), 23.1 (4), (6), (7))

This guide does not state current minimum wage amounts. The current rates are published by the Minister, and some classes of employees have rates set by regulation; the site does not yet hold a source for those rates or that regulation. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 23.1 (2), (7))

sections.heading: Hours of work, overtime and public holidays
paragraphs: No employer shall require or permit an employee to work more than “eight hours in a day” (or the employee's regular work day, if the employer set one longer than eight hours) and “48 hours in a work week”. The limits may be exceeded where the employee “has made an agreement with the employer”, and the Act sets conditions for such an agreement to be valid. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 17 (1)-(5))

An employer “shall pay an employee overtime pay of at least one and one-half times his or her regular rate for each hour of work in excess of 44 hours in each work week or, if another threshold is prescribed, that prescribed threshold.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 22 (1))

The Act lists the public holidays: New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, December 26, and “Any day prescribed as a public holiday”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 1 (1), “public holiday”)

If a public holiday falls on a day that would ordinarily be a working day and the employee is not on vacation, “the employer shall give the employee the day off work and pay him or her public holiday pay for that day.” The Act sets out exceptions and rules for agreeing to work on the holiday. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 26, 27)

sections.heading: Vacation and vacation pay
paragraphs: An employer shall give an employee a vacation of “at least two weeks after each vacation entitlement year that the employee completes, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “at least three weeks” if the period of employment is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 33 (1))

Vacation pay must equal at least “4 per cent of the wages, excluding vacation pay, that the employee earned during the period for which the vacation is given, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “6 per cent” if it is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 35.2)

sections.heading: Notice of termination or termination pay
paragraphs: “No employer shall terminate the employment of an employee who has been continuously employed for three months or more” unless the employer has given written notice under section 57 or 58 and the notice has expired, or has complied with section 61. The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay under this Part.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 54, 55)

Under the Act, an employer terminates employment if it “dismisses the employee or otherwise refuses or is unable to continue employing him or her”, if it “constructively dismisses the employee and the employee resigns from his or her employment in response to that within a reasonable period”, or if it lays the employee off for longer than a temporary lay-off. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 56 (1))

The notice period depends on the period of employment: “at least one week before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is less than one year”, rising by steps to “at least eight weeks before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is eight years or more.” Different rules apply when an employer terminates 50 or more employees at the employer's establishment in the same four-week period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 57, 58 (1))

Instead of notice, an employer may pay “termination pay in a lump sum equal to the amount the employee would have been entitled to receive under section 60 had notice been given”, and must continue benefit plan contributions for the notice period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 60 (1), 61 (1))

sections.heading: Severance pay
paragraphs: Severance pay is separate from termination pay. An employer who severs employment must pay it “if the employee was employed by the employer for five years or more” and one of two conditions is met. The first is that the severance came from a permanent discontinuance of all or part of the business at an establishment and the employee “is one of 50 or more employees who have their employment relationship severed within a six-month period as a result”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1))

The second is that “the employer has a payroll of $2.5 million or more”, measured as set out in subsection 64 (2). The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to severance pay under this section.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1), (2), (3))

Severance pay is calculated by multiplying “the employee's regular wages for a regular work week” by the completed years of employment plus completed extra months divided by 12. It “shall not exceed an amount equal to the employee's regular wages for a regular work week for 26 weeks.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 65 (1), (5))

sections.heading: Filing a complaint and its time limit
paragraphs: “A person alleging that this Act has been or is being contravened may file a complaint with the Ministry in a written or electronic form approved by the Director.” A complaint not filed in an approved form “shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (1), (2))

There is a limit for unionized workplaces. An employee represented by a trade union that is or was a party to a collective agreement “may not file a complaint alleging a contravention of this Act that is enforceable under subsection (1) or have such a complaint investigated.” Subsection 99 (1) makes the Act enforceable as if it were part of the collective agreement. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 99 (1), (2))

The Act sets a time limit: “A complaint regarding a contravention that occurred more than two years before the day on which the complaint was filed shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (3))

An employment standards officer investigating a complaint “may not issue an order for wages that became due to the employee” if “the wages became due more than two years before the complaint was filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 111 (1))

sections.heading: A complaint or a court case
paragraphs: The Act says “Subject to section 97, no civil remedy of an employee against his or her employer is affected by this Act.” An employee who starts a civil proceeding against the employer under the Act must serve notice on the Director, on a form approved by the Director, “on or before the date the civil proceeding is set down for trial.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 8 (1), (2))

An employee who files a complaint about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not commence a civil proceeding with respect to the same matter.” An employee who files a complaint claiming termination or severance pay “may not commence a civil proceeding for wrongful dismissal if the complaint and the proceeding would relate to the same termination or severance of employment.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (1), (2))

There is a withdrawal window: an employee who has filed a complaint may start a civil proceeding on those matters “if he or she withdraws the complaint within two weeks after it is filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (4))

It works the other way too. An employee who starts a civil proceeding about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not file a complaint with respect to the same matter”, and one who starts a proceeding for wrongful dismissal may not file a complaint for termination or severance pay about the same termination or severance. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 98 (1), (2))

CLEO's Steps to Justice has plain-language questions on these subjects, grouped under headings including “Getting paid”, “Getting fired or laid off” and “Claiming your rights as a worker”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Employment and work)
